claim.text: On a 3-layer fully-connected network with two hidden layers of 256 units each (784→256→256→10, ReLU activation, unit masking on the two hidden layers), trained with SGD (learning rate η=0.01) for 5 structural-edit cycles with 20 epochs per cycle, the GROW method as described in note 1 and the PRUNE method as described in note 2 produce closely matched winning-ticket final accuracy and winning-ticket trajectory-average accuracy across compactness budgets c∈{20,30,40,50}%, where c is the fraction of weights retained across growable and prunable layers, with no consistent ordering, on three benchmarks.
The GROW-PRUNE asymmetry is not inherent to sparsity or class-incremental training regimes.
The GROW-PRUNE asymmetry only becomes visible in harder feature-learning settings.

On CIFAR-100 (100-class classification, 50,000 training images, 10,000 test images, 32×32 color images) with a hybrid ConvNet consisting of a dense two-layer convolutional trunk (conv1: 3→32, k=3, p=1, ReLU, maxpool(2); conv2: 32→64, k=3, p=1, ReLU, maxpool(2); flatten to 4096) followed by a four-layer fully-connected head with unit-level masking (fc1: 4096→512, fc2: 512→512, fc3: 512→256, fc4: 256→100, ReLU, unit masking on fc1-fc3), trained with SGD (η=0.1) for 5 structural-edit cycles with 40 epochs per cycle, the GROW method (which starts from 10% of the target active-unit count and iteratively activates units using an activation-frequency heuristic (fraction of post-activation values exceeding τ=0.05), with no weight rewinding) achieves higher Cycle-ACC (test accuracy at the end of each structural-edit cycle during the GROW procedure) than PRUNE (iterative magnitude pruning starting from 100% active units, rewinding surviving weights after each pruning) at every compactness level c∈{20,30,40,50}%.

For the Cycle-ACC comparison between the GROW method (which starts from 10% of the target active-unit count and iteratively activates units using an activation-frequency heuristic (fraction of post-activation values exceeding τ=0.05), with no weight rewinding) and PRUNE (iterative magnitude pruning starting from 100% active units, rewinding surviving weights after each pruning), the Welch t-test p is < 0.001 at all compactness levels c∈{20,30,40,50}%.

The gap in Cycle-ACC (test accuracy at the end of each structural-edit cycle during the GROW procedure) between the GROW method (which starts from 10% of the target active-unit count and iteratively activates units using an activation-frequency heuristic (fraction of post-activation values exceeding τ=0.05), with no weight rewinding) and PRUNE (iterative magnitude pruning starting from 100% active units, rewinding surviving weights after each pruning) is increasing at higher compactness levels c∈{20,30,40,50}%.

On CIFAR-100, with the same hybrid ConvNet, after freezing the final mask discovered by each method, reinitializing the model weights, and retraining from scratch (Winning-Ticket evaluation following the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis protocol), GROW and PRUNE produce similar final accuracy across compactness levels c∈{20,30,40,50}%, with PRUNE slightly stronger at 40–50% compactness.
p > 0.05 at all compactness levels c∈{20,30,40,50}% for GROW vs. PRUNE final accuracy.

On CIFAR-100, with the same hybrid ConvNet, after freezing the final mask discovered by each method (GROW and PRUNE), reinitializing the model weights, and retraining from scratch (Winning-Ticket evaluation following the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis protocol), the GROW Cycle-ACC advantage observed during structural editing does not translate to clearly superior retrainable sparse architectures.

On CIFAR-100 (100-class classification, 50,000 training images, 10,000 test images, 32×32 color images) with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk: conv1 3→32, conv2 32→64, maxpool, flatten to 4096; four-layer fully-connected masked head: fc1 4096→512, fc2 512→512, fc3 512→256, fc4 256→100, ReLU, unit masking on fc1-fc3), PRUNE achieves higher Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy, the mean test accuracy across all structural-edit checkpoints during the pruning procedure) than GROW (activation-frequency-based unit activation from 10% active to target compactness, no rewind) at low and intermediate compactness.

On CIFAR-100 (100-class classification, 50,000 training images, 10,000 test images, 32×32 color images) with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk: conv1 3→32, conv2 32→64, maxpool, flatten to 4096; four-layer fully-connected masked head: fc1 4096→512, fc2 512→512, fc3 512→256, fc4 256→100, ReLU, unit masking on fc1-fc3), at c=50% compactness the two methods, PRUNE and GROW, are nearly tied in Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy, the mean test accuracy across all structural-edit checkpoints during the pruning procedure).

On CIFAR-100 (100-class classification, 50,000 training images, 10,000 test images, 32×32 color images) with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk: conv1 3→32, conv2 32→64, maxpool, flatten to 4096; four-layer fully-connected masked head: fc1 4096→512, fc2 512→512, fc3 512→256, fc4 256→100, ReLU, unit masking on fc1-fc3), under Winning-Ticket retraining (freezing final mask, reinitializing weights, retraining from scratch), differences in TAA (trajectory-average accuracy) between GROW (activation-frequency-based unit activation from 10% active to target compactness, no rewind) and PRUNE are not statistically significant at any compactness (p > 0.05).
The GROW-PRUNE separation lies in adaptive dynamics rather than final architecture quality.

On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), event-aligned cohort diagnostics computed on a single mini-batch at the moment of growth show that newborn units (units just activated by the GROW method) exhibit positive activation log-parity relative to incumbent units (units already active before growth), where log-parity is the natural logarithm of the ratio of mean per-unit activation rate (fraction of post-activation values exceeding a threshold τ on the mini-batch) for newborn units divided by that for incumbent units.

On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), event-aligned cohort diagnostics computed on a single mini-batch at the moment of growth show that newborn units (units just activated by the GROW method) exhibit strongly negative gradient log-parity (log ratio < 0), where gradient log-parity is the natural logarithm of the ratio of mean per-unit gradient magnitude (mean absolute pre-activation gradient |∂L/∂z_j| on the mini-batch) for newborn units divided by that for incumbent units (units already active before growth).
The growth bottleneck is a backward-pass integration problem rather than a dead-unit problem.

On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), over the training segment remaining after each growth event (within the same cycle), newborn GROW units' activation ratio (mean per-unit activation rate of newborn units divided by that of incumbent units, measured on a mini-batch) approaches or exceeds parity (ratio close to or above 1).

On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), over the training segment remaining after each growth event (within the same cycle), newborn GROW units' gradient ratio (mean per-unit gradient magnitude |∂L/∂z_j| of newborn units divided by that of incumbent units, measured on a mini-batch) remains far below parity (ratio < 1) throughout the entire cycle, including at the end-of-cycle checkpoint.

As claim 25 states, the backward-signal disadvantage is not merely a transient birth-time effect but persists over the available training horizon (the training segment remaining after each growth event within the same cycle) and limits how quickly newborn units can become useful.

On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), across all compactness levels c∈{20,30,40,50}% and intervention methods (vanilla GROW, Two-Speed—temporary learning-rate multiplier r>1 on newborn-associated parameters, Moment Transplant—copying optimizer buffers from a donor incumbent unit to newborn unit at birth, GradMax—gradient-based top-k selection of inactive units, Rand. Smooth-Leaky—a smoother randomized leaky activation function, Net2Wider—function-preserving widening by duplicating incumbent units), early gradient parity (mean natural logarithm of the ratio of per-unit gradient magnitude |∂L/∂z_j| for newborn units divided by that for incumbent units, averaged over the early post-birth training window) has a Spearman correlation of ρ = 0.88 with Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure).

On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), across all compactness levels c∈{20,30,40,50}% and intervention methods (vanilla GROW, Two-Speed—temporary learning-rate multiplier r>1 on newborn-associated parameters, Moment Transplant—copying optimizer buffers from a donor incumbent unit to newborn unit at birth, GradMax—gradient-based top-k selection of inactive units, Rand. Smooth-Leaky—a smoother randomized leaky activation function, Net2Wider—function-preserving widening by duplicating incumbent units), early activation parity (mean natural logarithm of the ratio of per-unit activation rate for newborn units divided by that for incumbent units, averaged over the early post-birth training window) has a Spearman correlation of ρ = 0.83 with Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure).
claim 27, claim 28 establish a strong quantitative link between the degree of newborn integration during early post-insertion training and the resulting trajectory-average adaptive performance.
Backward credit assignment is the primary newborn-integration bottleneck.

On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), among the evaluated interventions targeting the newborn integration bottleneck—Two-Speed (temporary learning-rate multiplier r>1 on newborn-associated parameters during warmup), Moment Transplant (copying optimizer buffers from a donor incumbent unit to newborn at birth), GradMax (gradient-based top-k selection of inactive units), Rand. Smooth-Leaky (a smoother randomized leaky activation function), and Net2Wider (function-preserving widening by duplicating selected incumbent units and redistributing outgoing weights)—GradMax-style gradient-based selection and Rand. Smooth-Leaky activation achieve the highest early integration parity (mean log-ratio of newborn-to-incumbent gradient magnitude and activation rate averaged over the early post-birth window) and the highest Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure).

On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), among the evaluated interventions targeting the newborn integration bottleneck, Two-Speed (temporary learning-rate multiplier r>1 on newborn-associated parameters during warmup) and Net2Wider (function-preserving widening by duplicating selected incumbent units and redistributing outgoing weights) provide weaker or less consistent relief across compactness levels.
Improving the integration of newborn units can strengthen adaptive-process performance (trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure).

On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), among the evaluated interventions targeting the newborn integration bottleneck, selection policy and activation-level trainability are the most effective levers.

On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), retrained-mask winning-ticket accuracy (accuracy after freezing the final mask, reinitializing model weights, and retraining from scratch) is not monotonically aligned with Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure) across intervention methods.

Methods that substantially improve edit-time integration (as measured by Cycle-TAA, i.e., trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure) do not necessarily produce better final retrainable subnetworks (as measured by retrained-mask winning-ticket accuracy, i.e., accuracy after freezing the final mask, reinitializing model weights, and retraining from scratch).

There is a lack of monotonic alignment in the Cycle-TAA vs. retrained-mask winning-ticket accuracy comparison across intervention methods, where Cycle-TAA is trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure and retrained-mask winning-ticket accuracy is accuracy after freezing the final mask, reinitializing model weights, and retraining from scratch.

Improved edit-time dynamics (as measured by Cycle-TAA, i.e., trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure) and final architecture quality (as measured by retrained-mask winning-ticket accuracy, i.e., accuracy after freezing the final mask, reinitializing model weights, and retraining from scratch) are distinct objectives that may require separate optimization criteria.

On class-incremental Split-CIFAR100 (CIFAR-100 partitioned into 10 tasks of 10 classes each, shared 100-way classifier head, no task-identity routing at test time, known task boundaries, fixed per-task training budget, structural edits at task boundaries separated by substantial optimization time), GROW combined with Rand. Smooth-Leaky activation (a smoother randomized leaky activation function) outperforms DENSE (full-capacity training without structural editing), PRUNE (iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding), and all other growth variants (vanilla GROW, GROW+TwoSpeed—temporary learning-rate multiplier on newborn parameters, GROW+MomentTransplant—copying optimizer buffers from donor to newborn, GROW+GradMax—gradient-based top-k selection, GROW+Net2Wider—function-preserving widening by unit duplication) in final accuracy.

Growth can be a competitive alternative to pruning in continual learning settings when newborn units have enough optimization time to integrate and are made more trainable through activation-level intervention.

Across five repeated-shift plasticity-stressing continual learning benchmarks—Permuted MNIST (500 tasks, 10,000 images/task, fixed random pixel permutation per task, 1 epoch per task), Random Label MNIST (50 tasks, 1,200 fixed images/task, fresh random labels per task, 400 epochs per task), Random Label CIFAR (50 tasks, 1,200 fixed CIFAR-10 images/task, fresh random labels per task, 400 epochs per task), 5+1 CIFAR (15 alternating hard/easy tasks from CIFAR-100, 780 update steps per task, classes do not repeat), and Continual ImageNet (500 binary classification tasks, 1,200 images/task from ImageNet downsampled to 32×32, classes do not repeat, 10 epochs per task)—PRUNE (iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding) is the strongest or near-strongest structural baseline (compared against DENSE and GROW-family methods) in settings with rapid distribution change.
Among growth-family methods, GROW combined with Rand. Smooth-Leaky (a smoother randomized leaky activation function) is the most robust growth variant.
GROW combined with Rand. Smooth-Leaky (a smoother randomized leaky activation function) consistently improves over vanilla GROW.
GROW combined with Rand. Smooth-Leaky (a smoother randomized leaky activation function) narrows the gap to PRUNE (iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding).

Among growth-family methods, GROW combined with Rand. Smooth-Leaky (a smoother randomized leaky activation function) is the only growth variant that becomes competitive with or outperforms PRUNE (iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding) in settings where structural events are separated by more optimization time.

Other birth interventions (Two-Speed—temporary learning-rate multiplier on newborn parameters, Moment Transplant—copying optimizer buffers from donor to newborn, GradMax—gradient-based top-k selection, Net2Wider—function-preserving widening by unit duplication) provide less consistent gains than GROW combined with Rand. Smooth-Leaky (a smoother randomized leaky activation function) across five repeated-shift plasticity-stressing continual learning benchmarks: Permuted MNIST (500 tasks, 10,000 images/task, fixed random pixel permutation per task, 1 epoch per task), Random Label MNIST (50 tasks, 1,200 fixed images/task, fresh random labels per task, 400 epochs per task), Random Label CIFAR (50 tasks, 1,200 fixed CIFAR-10 images/task, fresh random labels per task, 400 epochs per task), 5+1 CIFAR (15 alternating hard/easy tasks from CIFAR-100, 780 update steps per task, classes do not repeat), and Continual ImageNet (500 binary classification tasks, 1,200 images/task from ImageNet downsampled to 32×32, classes do not repeat, 10 epochs per task).

On a 3-layer fully-connected network with two hidden layers of 256 units each (784→256→256→10, ReLU activation, unit masking on the two hidden layers), trained with SGD (learning rate η=0.01) for 5 structural-edit cycles with 20 epochs per cycle, the GROW method as described in note 1 and the PRUNE method as described in note 2 produce closely matched winning-ticket final accuracy and winning-ticket trajectory-average accuracy across compactness budgets c∈{20,30,40,50}%, where c is the fraction of weights retained across growable and prunable layers, with no consistent ordering, on IID (independent and identically distributed) MNIST (10-class handwritten-digit classification, 60,000 training images, 10,000 test images, 28×28 grayscale), class-incremental Split-MNIST (5 tasks of 2 classes each, shared 10-way classifier head, no task-identity routing, Tiny Experience Replay buffer storing 50 samples per class), and the analogous Split-FashionMNIST setting.

On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), retrained-mask winning-ticket accuracy (accuracy after freezing the final mask, reinitializing model weights, and retraining from scratch) is not monotonically aligned with Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure) across the six intervention methods: vanilla GROW, Two-Speed, Moment Transplant, GradMax, Rand. Smooth-Leaky, and Net2Wider.

GradMax and Rand. Smooth-Leaky, which substantially improve edit-time integration (as measured by Cycle-TAA, i.e., trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure), do not necessarily produce better final retrainable subnetworks (as measured by retrained-mask winning-ticket accuracy, i.e., accuracy after freezing the final mask, reinitializing model weights, and retraining from scratch).

Among growth-family methods, GROW combined with Rand. Smooth-Leaky (a smoother randomized leaky activation function) is the only growth variant that becomes competitive with or outperforms PRUNE (iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding) in Split-CIFAR100.
